¶1 Auzubillah Minashaitan Nirajeem

¶2 Bismillah-ir-Rahman-ir-Rahim

¶3 We are going to discuss Sufi tariqa today. And this is of course, a concept that all of you probably have heard about that. If you want to be a Sufi, if you want to be a mystic, you have to belong to a tariqa otherwise, if you don't have a tariqa if you don't have a silsilah and if you don't have a Shaikh, it means that you cannot move into this journey towards Allah. Now, what does tariqa mean? The way they have translated in English of course, the literal meaning of tariqa is path. Therefore, the sufi tariqa is a path towards Allah. This is what we mean by tariqa. However, this concept has developed to be more than just a path.

¶4 It has developed lots of concepts around itself that has somehow rolled it out to be simply a path towards God. So, some have actually compared it with brotherhood's which existed in the West. So they say a Sufi tariqa is Sufi brotherhood where some people come together, they regard each other as brothers, they regard each other as members of the same culture or something like this. So this sufi tariqa is actually brotherhood, a fraternity. They are almost the same thing, the same concept and order which is a concept used in monastic practice, they have orders among themselves. In one Monastery, they come together and they have an order among themselves, they have people who work, people who organize and they have somehow compared a tariqa to an order.

¶5 But of course, these comparisons are just to give similarity between a tariqa which exists in the Sufi world and what has been practiced here in western mysticism. So I think the best thing is not to translate it to anything and just say that this is tariqa or a path towards Allah. Now what is a tariqa? I have two statements here. The emergence of the brotherhoods in reality meant the emergence of ‘elders’ with specific programmes of instruction, linked to a founder who is believed to have instituted their method and every brotherhood, now these are two main features of a tariqa has a ‘chain’, silsila, which is its pedigree of masters going back to the Prophet. Now in a sufi tariqa, when we say a sufi tariqa we think of the urafa that we have in Qum or Shia irfan is usually practiced in Sunni irfan.

¶6 We don't have such a thing as tariqa in Shia. As I explained before, the Shia faith is because of the concepts of Imamah would somehow not allow this type of silsilah issue to come in and even those people who are interested in the sheikhs are regarded as important as it is in sufi tariqa. Now, there are two features which are important in every tariqa. One, an elder who somehow initiates the type of instruction methods, which would make the wayfaring for many people easier. They find it very easy to work according to the method of this elder person. And therefore they come together, they come around the sheikh, the chef becomes the horse, the elder and is regarded to have extraordinary powers, extraordinary relationship with Allah.

¶7 They want to know what type of stations a person should, should carry on with until it comes to the final stages. So this is the most important concept. Now all major sufi tariqas have come about in seventh century. So before seventh century, you didn't have any tariqa. It means that, although had great mystics some of whom we discussed in the previous session, there is not such a thing as a tariqa. And this was something which was invented later on when people felt that rather than relying on their own practices they needed some instructors to tell them what to do. And the second very important issue about tariqa is that all of them claim that they gain the knowledge the silsilah from the prophet.

¶8 Now this is something which is mainly a Shia idea, that the knowledge of the prophet is transferable. Well, we believe through inheritance, the knowledge of the prophet is transferable through inheritance to Aimamah. And that's why we do not regard Aimamah as ordinary for example, Imam Ali as an ordinary companion of the Prophet and any companion having any type of knowledge however knowledgeable they might be, they don't have this type of inheritance. It means them and the prophet in terms of gaining the knowledge of the prophet and having the same knowledge, the same rank, the same procedure of receiving knowledge from Allah as the prophet is going to have. So, the idea of a tariqa is that although they do not believe in Imam, they believe that there should be an authority receiving the esoteric knowledge of the prophets.

¶9 All other companions received the exoteric knowledge of the prophet, knowledge of sharia, knowledge of exegesis and other issues. But the knowledge of Prophet was not restricted to his own. It was as well a knowledge which should have been gone from heart to heart. And that was the most important issue here. And therefore they said, okay, the sheikh, there is a chain which receives this knowledge from the prophet from that sheikh comes to the following sheikh from that sheikh to the following sheikh, of course it's not an orderly type of transference of knowledge because in Shia faith we believe that it is a true Messiah and there is a line of Imams. This was quite clear at the time of the Prophet.

¶10 In this case vaguely close to the idea of Shia knowledge, concept of knowledge of the Aimmah. And that is why usually, as we studied before, they say that Sufism is just a branch of Shiaism in Sunni faith. It is just a cult of Shia in the Sunni world. They just have imported the concept of Shia into the Sunni world, they believe in Abu Bakr, Omar and Jamaah and all these things, but what they actually have is a type of Shia faith among them. So this is, so far a tariqa. Usually a sheikh appoints someone else's after himself and they do have conflicts. As we have conflicts even in the time of Imams you see, although we believe that Imams would appoint an Imam.

¶11 The next imam would have conflicts after every imam that some people claim imamah for themselves. Here as well yes, there are lots of conflicts in every silsilah or tariqa about who should be the heir to the previous sheikh. Now, then the sub-tariqas options, of course, as you see now, there are many, many names of tariqas around the world. Most of which are offshoots of six to seven tariqas, which were brought about in the seventh or eighth century. And this was an age what was probably we need to research in this or a deep investigation, what was the reason that these tariqas appeared, popped up in the seventh century and eighth century, in the Sunni world.

¶12 Now, then, the sub-tariqa usually when we had a big personality showing up in a specific tariqa, whose influence was more powerful than the founder of that tariqa. Then a sub-tariqa was found and the tariqa was called after that influential person. So is a path within another path within the chain of a given brotherhood, particularly strong and effective personality may well produce a sub-brotherhood. His forcefulness may provide a new series of teachings or the revival of old one. Usually when a sub-tariqa is formed, that influential person would come into conflict with some of the teachings of the elder or would bring some new teachings which was evolution arise the whole system of method of instruction, and therefore a sub-tariqa is formed.

¶13 Now, most commonly, this will be reflected in a double barrel label embodying the name of the two founders, for example the Naqshbandi Tariqa in the 11th century was somehow revived in India by Shaykh Ahmad Sirhindi, who was the Mujaddid. So he founded the Mujaddid Tariqa and that was Mujaddid Naqshbandi Tariqa certainly. So they had a double type of label with themselves and the sub brotherhood may later achieve such great importance that the name of the original brotherhood is lost. We have this for example, in of course, not that the original brotherhood will go away. But those people who follow the sub-tariqa never attribute themselves anymore to the original one. For example now we have the Noorbakshiyya around the world which is very corrupt by that tariqa but it came out of originally sort of Suhrawardiyya.

¶14 And now of course the Noorbakshiyya, they don't call themselves Suhrawardiyya because the teachings are completely different. However, of course, it says in history that they were an offshoot of this. Now, we might have a type of several stages. There's one example here I have given Suhrawardiyya which gave rise to Kubrawiyya because of the very influential formidable Najm al-Din Kubra. Then there are some options of Noorbakshiyya as well now around the world are very difficult thing to remember. In later centuries it is common for a Muslim to belong to two or more parts at the same time and engage in practices which are forbidden in for example, it is forbidden in Naqshbandi, but someone belongs to Naqshbandi can act according to the instruction of Naqsband and also belong say for example, to Suhrawardiyya which allows Sima and to listens to music, for example.

¶15 Sima is, usually in old days, they say what would help the refinement of the soul is good preaching. So, usually when the Sufis came together, there was a good teacher who preached then they said, this good preaching should be accompanied by a nice rhythmic voice and it is now common especially in Iran. If you go to any Sufi circle, you will see when they come together, they start to recite, for example, poems of Hafez which is of course very highly dreaded among Sufis in Iran or Saudi or others. And they do it with a very nice voice. Now, some people did not allow this. Even it was very nice, with targih which they say, is allowed or not.

¶16 And then, in some Sufi tariqa, they said, if this is accompanied by some sort of news, it would be more effective, refine the soul to divert the attention towards the harmony of this, because all these harmonies have some effect in the attention of the soul towards something. So they said, of course now, for us music is something very common, we listen to all sorts of music and poetry and songs and all these things. In old days, there was great controversy that whether this was allowed or not, and especially among Shias, one of the things with which they attacked Sufis was that they have sessions in which they sit and listen to music and listen to poetry and to nice voice.

¶17 So I think nowadays, it's quite common for us and the world has changed completely, especially after these fatwa about music. So this was the concept of Sima.

¶18 So it was forbidden in one tariqa, it was allowed in another type of tariqa and therefore, this controversy. I know some people who, who they say for example, they have ijaza, that's a permission to instruct others in this sufi tariqa from almost all tariqas existing in the world. And how this is possible, I don't know because these instructions, some sometimes come against each other. They are contradicting. You cannot practice all of them together. And for example, the prominent Sufi travels around the world, okay. And he needs heads of these tariqas. Just in a meeting, as an honorary type of compliment, they say, Okay, I permit you to instruct anyone who wants to become a Sufi.

¶19 And in this way, they gain ijaza of that tariqa to instruct. And so it comes and it somehow makes the whole tarifa issue ineffective, isn't it? Because then there is no meaning if you have ijaza to instruct people according to all tariqas then the whole concept of tariqa goes away. So this is now how it has become. And of course, the concept of tariqa has lost weight very much in recent centuries. It was very powerful after seventh century when it was founded throughout until the a few centuries ago and now it has somehow lost its importance because people have become more probably engrossed in studying about Islam and finding their own methods of practice, rather than listening to a sheikh.

¶20 And especially listening to one person now is not very much pleasure with submitting oneself completely to a person because one of the most important assets of tariqa is that you have to completely submit to the sheikh, whatever he says whatever he does and this is why you see because Ismailis are is very much influenced by this Sufi tariqa and their faith has become a type of tariqa itself. And that's why you see, for example, Agha Khan does whatever he wants, and he indulges in all types of pleasures. And theoretically, the members of the Ismaili faith cannot object because they say he is the imam but they have to completely submit to whatever the imam does.

¶21 As they say, as someone who's being washed, being done ghusl-mayyat for example, lying before someone who makes this ghusl was completely powerless. The person who's before someone who needs the ghusl, he tells them whatever he wants and washes them whatever way he wants. They say, a person should submit to an instructor or sheikh in the same way, possibly someone who performs the ghusl. So just like a dead person, before someone who performs ghusl. This is how you have to be in front of sheikh. Now it's very difficult for modern mind to accept this isn't it?

¶22 Q1. Not audible Ans: In Shiaism, it’s not a tariqa type of thing. They don’t follow a tariqa. They find an instructor for themselves. And that instructor doesn't come from any tariqa or doesn't have any special ijazah of instruction from someone else. The thing which is said Syed Ali Kazmini is very of course heavy because he says you don't go into a tariqa to find a sheikh. But you look how your life for someone in whom you could trust, you could entrust your soul actually. So it is somehow finding a knowledgeable person who could tell you but that knowledgeable person of course you can't, you can't know by their writing or what they have studied because this is not something which comes into that category.

¶23 You have to make sure that these people have themselves, actually have a journey along the path. So that when you come to pitfall they can tell you because during this journey, the souls and nafs could come into very strange attitudes and position that the person doesn't know what this means, what they have to do now. Should they for example, it comes time that you hate worship, it comes time that you hate living the society, for example. These are all different attitudes of the soul during this journey. And if someone has already travelled through this, he can tell you, you can go and tell them that now I feel like this. Especially I was reading some of the writings of Ayatullah Hassanzadeh, he himself says that I came across many experiences that I didn't know what they were.

¶24 And I just went through Allamah Tbatatabi and I told him this is how I feel and very easily he explained for me, what you have to do next. What does this mean? And especially some experiences, which I hadn't, I mean experiences without persons; these are the most difficult ones that they come through. And if they don't know what to do next, what's the meaning of this then they get lost. So this is when the existence of this sheikh is necessary. What these tariqa say? They say that for saying that you need someone to instruct initially, which is something we don't have in our Shia faith. Of course, when you come to some attitudes, that great sheikh will tell you what that would benefit you now, okay, whether Allahu Akbar is good to say or La ilaha illalah is good to say.

¶25 These are for different positions that the sole arises. However, initially just these tariqas say that you come to us and I tell you what to do what to say. And if you say anything without our instructions, you are tending to get lost on the path which is something of an exaggeration of these instructors. Now, the major tariqas which came about in the seventh century, we have the Qadarriya Tariqa which is the very famous one. And then Suhrawardiyya Tariqa and then Shadhiliyya Tariqa, Naqshbandiyya, Kubrawiyya. Chishtiya and Tijaniya Tariqa. These are all Sunni tariqas. We have the Shia tariqa which I will discuss later on. So, these are all Sunni tariqas which were prevailing from seventh to eighth ninth century.

¶26 Now we will discuss about Qadariyya.

¶27 Qadariyya Now this silsilah was Abd al-Qadir Jilani. Now, again, also he was from Iran. Didn't I tell you? So this man was actually from my north of Iran. And, of course, he was brought up later on in Baghdad and that was where he flourished in his knowledge. He studied Humbali Fiqh at the age of 17 and his conversion to Sufism occurred at the hand of the stern Sufi Master called Abu'l-Khair Hammad ibn Muslim al-Dabbas. Now, these Sufis actually were very strong everywhere in the Muslim world and usually with one Muslim world divided into Sunni and Shia, I think we do not see the totality of other divisions which go in the Muslim world. By one other division, you could divide the Muslim world of course into Shias, Sufis and Sunnis and then if you have studied the history, you will see how great influence the Sufis have actually exerted during the history whether Sunni or Non-Sunni, they were very powerful especially with the king.

¶28 And many decisions taken by kings, by rulers, by the Khulafa were actually under the instruction of these elders of the Sufi tariqa especially after seventh century. And the reason is clear, because these people were people of some extraordinary power and the kings were inclined to listen to them because sometimes they knew okay, they said things about the future and in this way, they somehow exerted a great influence on kings. Now, they used to convert many people to Sufism, actually and this Jilani, who actually had come to learn Humbali which is very different from Sufi type of learning, was converted into Sufism. In 521, at the age of 50, at the age of 17 he went to Baghdad.

¶29 Later on, he converted to Sufism. And he had a type of success in life until the age of 50, where he became a great mystic. Then, following the dream that urged him to impart his knowledge to the people he returned to social life and became a fiery Humbali preacher. Now, Abd al-Qadir himself, although he had great power, extreme powers due to his, of course his Sufi fame he regarded himself mostly as a preacher. However, later on of course, they started to establish a tariqa after his name, his students because they knew what type of powers and spiritual charisma he had. His principal was, is that which is sufficient for the secret of the past….. He was not a solicit writer.

¶30 He was just an instructor actually. And one year was a standard exposition of the ethical and moral precepts incumbent on the Sunni Muslim. However, it was criticized by eminent Ibne Taymiyah for this mystical listening, and super irrigates react. Of course, Ibne Taymiyah he was the greatest enemy of Sufis, you know that, and actually, when he came forward to oppose many types of bidaat as in his own terminology, the first thing was, of course, the bidaat of Sufi and then Shia and then no one I think was saved from his attacks as committing bidaat. His shrine in Baghdad was rebuilt by the order of the Ottoman Sultan Suleiman nine, I don't know whether anyone has visited Abdullah Qadar’s shrine in Baghdad.

¶31 I haven't been there, but they say it's quite close to Abu Hanifa tomb. And many people go and visit his shrine as the moment. And his tariqa continues to be used widely in India, Pakistan subcontinent and Turkey. One of the most powerful qadariyya tariqa even now among Indian Muslims, his name is invoked whenever cholera or any other epidemic strikes a certain area or city. I read this. I don't know whether it be India, this is a case of course amongst Sunni and not among the Shias. He has great respect amongst Sunni.

He attacked the Ismaili’s in the name of all Shia worlds. And that's why even though Shias could not act I mean, the Ishna Ashari ulema, of course Allahma.. had lots of discussions and wrote books against his writing, but he absolutely hated whatever was going on in the large world, Ismaili and Ishna Ashari. Therefore, people thought he is genius and he is has come with articulates against Shias and other. And also, of course, there were lots of bidaat going around that he had but 80% of what he said was wrong.

¶35 Suhrawardiyya

¶36 Of course, there were two suhrawardies. One was Abū al-Najīb Abd al-Qādir Suhrawardī and then his nephew and student Omar Suhrawardi who was actually the main founder of the tariqa, the second one. Shahabuddin Omar Suhrawardi. We have another Shahabuddin Suhrawardi, who is the founder of the aluminous philosophy. You should not be mistaken between these two because that was Shia Shahabuddin and he is Sunni Shahabuddin Suhrawardi. They are very close in the name. The Suhrawardiyya tariqa, of course, was founded by the uncle Abū al-Najīb Abd al-Qādir Suhrawardī. He was born about 497 in Sohrevard in Iran again very close to my hometown in Iran and faces genealogists the first type Abu Bakr. However, although they trace their genealogy to Abu Bakr it's very interesting because all these tariqas take the chain from Imam Ali (as) to the prophet and they say he's the one who has given us all this knowledge.

¶37 Except Naqshbandiyya, who traces their genealogy from Imam Sadiq (as) and he says that the knowledge goes through Abu Bakr to the prophet. It is an irony that the Shias has created in this way. He studied with Abu Hamid Al-Ghazali in Esfahan. Now this Abu Hamid Al-Ghazali is different from Muhammad Al Ghazali who was his elder brother and he was a Sufi and more mystical than Muhammad Al Ghazali himself. Of course, Muhammad Al Ghazali was a moderate Sufi if you want to know, what the attributes of a Sufi were in the fifth and sixth century and what the teaching were. The best reference, a moderator is Ahya Uloom-ud-Din which is, of course, a very resourceful book, a very influential book instructive, but full of rubbish.

¶38 I mean, there lots of rubbish things in this book, really, I mean, if you go through, you will see that this type of Hades, that he recalls the type of anecdotes that he brings about the facilities. I mean, it's amazing how this great man could have revealed these issues.

¶39 Q3. Not audible

¶40 Ans: No, of course not. Ghazali himself of course, was quite sincere and very knowledgeable, and he's speaking about Allah are very, very resourceful. But the issue is that he relied on anecdotes, and a hadith, which were really unreliable. And he just wrote them to preach people.

¶41 Now what has been done in the Shia world because some Shia scholars believe that Ghazali converted to Shiaism at the end of life. And this is very much promoted by Faisal Kashani, who somehow refined Ahya Uloom-ud-Din and made a book, which is a refinement of that that book and causes the refinement of Ahya Uloom-ud-Din called as the revival of Ahya Uloom-ud-Din, the revival of the revival because Ahya Uloom-ud-Din means revival of the sciences of religion. And then he calls his book revival of the revival of the sciences of the religion. And what he says in the introduction is that, he always says, Abu Hamid (ra) was a great man, whatever he has written in this book is really useful to read and achieve.

¶42 I mean, sometimes you read passages from Ahya Uloom-ud-Din and you cannot help yourself to be to be influenced by that part. Now, he said he was quite an influential man very sincere, but unfortunately, before he became a Mustabshir towards the end of his life, he relied on a hadith and an anecdote which are quite nonsense, not being understood because they are not something to be relied upon.

¶43 Q3. Who is a Mustabshir?

¶44 Ans: It is someone who finds insight and usually the Shias say to hope whoever converts from Sunnism to Shiaism, they call him a Mustabshir who found insights in a sense.

¶45 Now, he says, So, I have tried to refine the book, he has omitted lots of those anecdotes and hades that he did not believe in and instead he has added a hades from aimmah that of course, Ghazali did not bring in and therefore his book Tahzibul Ahya ia called Al Mahjatul Bayzah, the clear path. The right path in the refinement of the Ahya Uloom-ud-Din. It has become a treasure actually. The book is written by Faisal Kashani. We are translating the book in Islamic college because it's huge book. And it's something that's really needed in our mother tongue and I was saying that Mohammed Al Ghazali, he was a moderate mystic. You go through his book, Ahya Uloom-ud-Din you see that is full of nonsense, nonsensical statements.

¶46 Now this brother Ahmed Al Ghazali, he was a traitor. He has a very, very strange idea. He was more well known in the world of mysticism than Muhammad Al Ghazali. One of the things that he was of course very stringent in following Al Hallaj and the intoxicated mystics of that time. And one of the things which has actually given rise to a tariqa which you still have this, especially in some parts of Iran, I have seen these people, a tariqa in which they worship shaytaan. Now, why they worship shaytaan or they respect, they're called Yazidi as well as they say, because Ahmed Al Ghazali was of the opinion that shaytaan is the first muwahid in the world.

¶47 Why because although Allah settled that he will punish him, he did not accept to make sajdah to anyone but Allah. And then, of course, actually was created here. Now, they had some sort, of course very embellished type of literature to promote. But what it has given rise to now that some people just adore shaytaan and they are called shaytaan parast or the people who are devoted to shaytaan. In western Iran, we have some of them in especially we have a city called Carolyn's near the border of Iraq. All the people in that city are shaytaan parast because they came from this order of Sufis who actually adored shaytaan for his monotheism. Now is there any argument against Ahmed Al Ghazali who said that he was the first and the most faithful monothesit in this world.

¶48 He did not accept the prophet before anything or anyone but God, although got punished, in a sense shaytaan said you punish me, or you reward me. I'm not going to worship anyone but you. It was obedience, which was important but he said, you want me to worship someone other than you? But by obeying you I'm actually betraying my faith in you or betraying my love for you. And I'm not going to betray my love because you tell me, you put me in hell, I'm not going to betray my love for you.

¶55 Now this sukrawardi on his return to Baghdad, he became a disciple of Hammad al-Dabbas which of course, was the instructor of Jilani as well. And this Hammad al-Dabbas had great influence on the development of later mystical thoughts. And just like Ghazali himself, he taught at Nizammiyya while he was a sufi and among his students were Ibn al-Asakir who was a very famous author in the history of Damascus and al-Sam’ani another very famous historian. So although he was a Sufi, he was very much respected in terms of jurisprudence, in terms of theology and other issues such like Ghazali before he left Nizamiyya. You know, what nizamiyya means. Anyone knows what this I mean? These were actually schools of theology, which were built at the time of the Abbasid era by the formidable vazir Kazi Nizamul Mulk and that's why they were called Nizamiyyah and these schools became like Oxford and Cambridge.

¶56 I mean, anyone who teaches in Nizamiyya was an Oxbridge man. And you would see that any prominent person whoever had taught in Nizamiyya, in their CV or in their record is written that they taught for a while in Nizamiyya. And it showed that the excellence and the standards of their knowledge because the people who were chosen to teach there were really knowledgeable people. His fame is largely due to his disciple and nephew Shihab al-Din Abu Hafs Umar al-Suhrawardi (not to be confused by Shihab al-Din Yahya Suhrawardi the Illuminationist philosopher) who was the true founder of Suhrawardiyya and the author of the last classical sufi manual Awarif al-Ma’arif. This man has both the kuniya and the name of Umar Bin Khattab.

¶57 This tariqa is best known for the practice of perpetually deciding the formula La Ilaha Illallah. Now wherever you go and talk about sukrawardiyya they have a very famous practice. Perpetually they say La Ilaha Illalah and that's why sukrawardiyya very popular amongst Shia mystics because Shia mystics as well say that it is best to say all the time La Ilaha Illalah. Now, of course, they say for two reasons. One reason is because of course the greatest it possesses itself and the other because it is zikrul khatib. If I say La Ilaha Illalah three times, now you cannot realise. I say that, you cannot realise and they say, this is good, this is zikrul khatib. But when you say SubhanAllah everyone knows that you're saying the zikr.

¶58 See, everyone realizes that you are saying the zikr although you want to hide everyone realizes, so they say, among Shia mystics, especially this is zikr, isn’t it? It is very popular because usually people try to show off that they are people of zikr especially if they have a tasbeeh and all the time they say Subhanallah. And they say, if you want to show off the best zikr is Subhanallah because everyone can hear, okay. But if you want to hide the best zikr is La Ilaha Illalah. Now this of course, tariqa is well known for this zikr until the remembrance of the tongue becomes a remembrance of the hearts, then the heart becomes empty of everything and God manifests itself within it.

¶59 Of course, they have techniques for doing this. Now, the whole issue of tariqas are these techniques that they instruct to their followers, for example, they say, when you want to say La Ilaha Illalah, first of all you have to say for a long time and then you have to be in a dark room and then you have to sit in a specific position. And then you have to say with a specific rhythm and all these instructions they give so that they can somehow contemplate that this zikr goes from the tongue to the heart, and the heart starts to be the same rhythm of La Ilaha Illalah. And then gradually the soul would pick it up and the soul would become familiar with this La Ilaha Illalah and it will become a permanent habit of the soul to think about that there is no God but Allah.

¶60 So, this tariqa is well known for this La Ilaha Illalah. Suhrawardiyya emphasizes the importance of the canonical prayer, dhikr and fasting of Ramadan and all other types of sharia’s. So, they are completely abiding by the rules of Sharia. Now modification of the dhikr exercised along the lines of Yogic mysticism, as I said when you want to say this zikr you have to sit in a specific position, which is very similar to yogic mysticism that the positioning of the body is very important in this practice of suhrawardiyya which is practiced by Chishtiyya in India of course. In Naqshbandiyya these are very important the yogic type of mysticism.

¶61 Naqshbandiyya

¶62 Now, we come to Naqshbandiyya which is the most important cemetery in the Muslim world, the most powerful and the most the biggest enemy of all Shias around the world. So if you find a naqshbandi do not tell them that you are Shia because they will kill you to go to paradise. This is the standard of course. Now this Sufi, he's not from Iran and of course this hatred for Shiaism is not somehow promoted by Naqshband himself. It was later on developed by his students. He got his name from a type of embroidery because Naqshbandi means someone who creates Naqsh, creates imprints. So he wasn't an embroider however, his name is more commonly taken to refer to fixing, in the purified tablet of the heart, of the imprint of the name Allah by means of a silent and permanent dhikr.

¶63 But this is of course something made up later on that why he was called Naqshabandi because he imprints the name of Allah in the hearts. His descent is attributed to Imam Ja’far al-Sadiq (as) and ironically he takes back his silsila through Abu Bakr and through Abu Bakr to the prophet and he was known in his birth place Bukhara, ad Khaaji-e Balaa gardaan, “the averter of disaster” because well as Shias of course, they do tawassul to their imam and then the bala or disaster, the followers or other good people of Naqshbandi do tawassul to this Baha’ al-Din Muhammad b. Muhammad Naqshband or Khaaji-e Balaa gardaan, “the averter of disaster”.

¶64 He was an associate of Ghazan Khan, the Mongol ruler for some time. And of course, through the influence of Ghazan Khan he succeeded to convert many people around the Islamic world into this Naqshbandi tariqa and that's how it is very powerful. He is buried in Bukhara in Qasr-i Hinduwan the hamlet in which he was born and was called later on Qasr-i Aarifan out of respect for him. Now what are the characteristics of Naqshbandi? 1. Emphasis on a silent ‘remembrance of God’ as opposed to the usual practice of repeating a formula aloud. So they do not allow you to make a formula to go somewhere and say they are very social. The naqshabandi are very socially inclined.

¶65 And you see that how, actually, the instructions of a aarif are different. I mean, you could be social and you could be an aarif. You could be secluded and you could be an aarif, you could say zikr loudly or you could be an RF and you could say the zikr in your heart, you could be an aarif. If all these methods work, it means that there is no one single method for practicing irfan. It means that human beings can adapt themselves to any type of situation to go to Allah and I think the instructions should be not in terms of these techniques, these are not very important. And this is why you don't find these techniques in Shia irfan that you should say loudly or silently or you should say like this or like that, is not very important.

¶66 In Shiaism what they say, they say that you are like, the type of channel your soul, is the channel to Allah. Now, in this channel or a canal or river, every river which goes to Allah is different. So, when you try to travel in this path different people come to different experience, especially this is very much stressed by Shia urafa as they say, you do not expect that you travel along this path, you get the same experiences as other people. You might find completely different experiences. Now, this is very strange thing, when you when you drop a coin on top of this, it will make sound for a long while. Now, very strangely some Sufi they say that when they pass through some station, they found this type of sound in their hearts like coins dropping on to of this.

¶67 And for a long time, they find this repeating and many Sufis have been after the sound in their hearts, why it doesn't happen to us? And of course, this is an example this is an outstanding example given that look, you don't have to get these sounds because people are very different, as their faces are different, as their taste are different. When they start to go through a path of irfan their experiences are completely different especially this is important, I mean, we when you go through this path, you realize that how different human beings are and we are not photocopies of each other. We are completely different rivulet coming from Allah. Now, what they say is that this rivulet is made or this type of channel or canal is made so that there is a permanent flow of pain of grace from Allah to you and this is non-stoppable.

¶68 This doesn't stop at all. It always comes and this is actually the purpose of the creation. It says people are always in dispute except on those upon whom Allah has favoured His mercy. And then he says it is just a favour or mercy upon you that you have been created not for anything else. So, they say this canal to Allah is there to receive that permanent flow of grace from Allah and that is permanent knowledge coming, permanent light coming. Now, the only thing is that you blocked this by your actions, you block this by your depths, which comes into this channel, like all kinds of different dirt going to river and blocking the passage of the water.

¶69 They say this is a good analogy actually. They say the main purpose of traveling through this path of irfan is to somehow cleaning this channel, putting away the heat, putting away the blockage so that the flow of grace would come to you. Now, that flow of grace would come to you but it will take your shape. It is very important. It will take your own shape. You are a vessel which is completely different in shape from other vessels. And when that grace comes into you it takes your own shape and it becomes very beautiful and people will look at each other inshallah in jannah everyone's grace is different from other people grace. Grace is one but it has come into different types of containers and it would have found very, very beautiful types of shapes and colour.

¶70 And I don't know whether you have heard about that the ways to Allah is as many number of the people. Now some people use this hades to say, there's not one way, you can have any religion, you can choose your own way. This is a wrong interpretation. The right interpretation is that when you practice Islam or recite the Quran, you do your Salah, but the experience and the way that we can find towards Allah is through all these is different from the experience of the person sitting next to you because you are different. It's just like eating fruit. The taste that I get from that fruit certainly you don't get that taste from the same fruit because of the whole construction of your body or the whole construction of the system on the tasting and all these things are different.

¶71 So when it comes to mystical experience that will show itself more outstanding. That's why these experiences and these instructions are not very much of course. Everyone should go in the same way. Everyone should find his or her own suitable type of practice and worship. So here the emphasis is on pity. And this is because of course the experience of Naqshband himself was like this. And then he wanted to somehow extend this experience to other people.

¶72 2. Denunciation of dancing and listening to music

¶73 Now dancing of course, not dancing that they do now days. It is a type of mystical dance that they did the way Islam. Now we have the Mevlevi as they call it Turkey. And I don't know whether you have seen that. How they dance and go around. They do a type of very harmonious dance and they say this is a symbolic type of movement which will again remind you of Allah. Again this is completely denounced by naqshbandiyya.

¶74 3. Deprecation of charismatic feats and saintly miracles (karaamaat)

¶75 This is very much rebuked in this naqshbandi. This is a type of very ascetic type of life which they somehow advertise.

¶76 4. Keeping pious company (suhbah) and avoiding retreats (khalwah)

¶77 5. Fidelity to shari’a in social, political and devotional life

¶78 And this why you find many naqshbandi sufi becoming political leaders in the Arab world, especially in Africa, Indo-Pakistan and many who are very active politically. Most of the prominent people of naqsbandi tariqa great politicians as well.

¶79 6. Marked hostility to Shii Islam (developed probably after Baha’ al-Din). This is the only tariqa which does not trace its silsila back to Ali (a)

¶80 7. Rejection of Ibn Arabi’s theory of wahdat al-wujood

¶81 This is very close to philosophy and of course theory of wahdat al-wujood is something which cannot be understood by a simple mind. And these people were very intellectual. They rejected the theory of wahdat al-wujood.

¶82 Distinguishing features they say a person should have 3 awarness:

¶83 1- wuquf-i zamaani: “temporal awareness,” the constant examination of one’s state during dhikr that how they have improved by saying all these zikr and these are very important in the sense that they check their improvement after each session of zikr.

¶84 2- wuquf-i ‘adadi: “numerical awareness,” the enumeration of the times dhikr is performed in order to discourage the intrusion of distracting thoughts. That means they do not a tasbeeh during zikr. They try to remember because the number of zikr is of course very important. Especially in sufi tariqa it is very important. How many times you mention a zikr and because when you use the tasbeeh you mind goes here and there because tasbeeh is counting for you. They say that you have to concentrate in your mind on counting this zikr and therefore your mind wouldn't be distracted by other contemplation and other thoughts. I don’t know how seful that could be because then whole attention is diverted towards counting.

¶85 I just don't know how they do it. It is very difficult. But it is possible, you can say 100 times without tasbeeh and just counting in your mind and maybe after a while you will become use to this way that you will count in your mind somehow paying attention to counting as well as attention to the zikr. It's not a bad method because at least it doesn't let you to think about your business, think about other issue etc. Just concentrate on counting. You have to bring it into balance of counting and thinking about the meaning of zikr as well.

¶86 3- wuquf-I qalbi: “awareness of the heart,” the direction of attention to the physical heart in order to make it participate in the work of dhikr

¶87 This is the most important and this you can find have penetrated into other sufi tariqas as well and that is awareness of the heart in the direction of attention to the physical heart in order to make it participate in the work of dhikr. Now they say how they do it, they say that when you say La Ilaha Illalah for example, you have to somehow give all your attention to this physical heart in a sense that you say La Ilaha Illalah but you have an eye on the heart as well. And when we say attention of the heart or awareness of the heart, it doesn't mean the way we says that you haven't heard your heart.

¶88 No, you have to think about your physical heart. Try to do this maybe it will work for you. You try to somehow divert your attention to the heart so that gradually you try to imagine that it is not you who is saying La Ilaha Illalah. It is your heart which is saying it. It comes from your heart. Now they have a method by sukrawardi or naqshbandi, they say you sit in a quiet place and you have to sit cross legged okay. And then you imagine your heart and then what you do, you say La Ilaha you take your breath in and then when you say Illalah you take your breath out. Some Shia mystics as well have advised this of course not all of them.

¶89 Some of them say that it is a nice way of saying zikr and they say that they have hades from Imam Ali (as) advising this. I don’t know whether it is authentic or not. When you say Illalah you empty yourself from everything except Allah but bringing out the own Ila that exist inside you. These are three very important techniques used by naqshbandi when they want to say zikr. The mujaddidi sub-branch of Naqshbandiyya was established in India by Shaykh Ahmad Sirhindi (d. 1034/1624), known as the mujaddid (Renewer).

¶90 Q6. Not audible

¶91 Ans: Yes, I have seen the hades from Imam Ali (as) and the other from Imam Reza (as) regarding this type of zikr. But they are not very reliable. They might be made up. If you see something that are made by Sufis in the past, you cannot rely on them.
